full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. -This appeal by special leave .is directed against the judgment and order passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in F.A. No. 61 of 1979 modifying the decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Title Suit No. 155 of 1978. 

 3. The plaintiff alleged that the Pourashava seat Police force on 6.5.73 and he was evicted forcibly. He suffered a loss of Tk. 49,000/- and loss of his reputation for which he brought the suit. The suit was decreed by trial court for a sum of Tk. 99,400/- but, it was dismissed as against defendants 1 to 3, namely, Pourashava, its Administrator and the Magistrate and also defendants 8 and 9, namely, Officer of the District Council and the District Council. 

 4. Defendant No. 4 appealed before the High Court Division. The High Court Division on consideration of evidence affirmed the decree and allowed the appeal in part modifying to the extent that the plaintiff is entitled to Tk. 50,000/- for damage and Tk. 25,000 for the loss of his reputation with interest. 

 6. The suit was filed on 1.9.73. As noticed the suit is for declaration of tenancy. When we asked the plaintiff respondent's Counsel as to the nature of the suit and whose tenancy he was claiming between 16.9.72 to 1 .9.71 and to whom he paid rent, the Counsel had no answer. It is very unfortunate that the courts below decreed the suit which on the face of it warrants no such declaration. The plaintiff was clearly a trespasser. When a notice of Nadabi Muktipatra and transfer in favour of defendants Nos. 4 to 7 were served upon him, he did not astern defendant No.4 as a new landlord nor he paid any rent to the Pourashava either. He simply squatted on the premises. He was evicted forcibly according to him though he has given a receipt showing receipt of his all belongings from the suit premises, Ext. Chha (1). No doubt, hedisowned this Ext. by saying that the signatures were obtained on the blank sheet of papers. The Trial Court, no Doubt found that the receipt was obtained by force and consequently recorded a finding that "a bona fide bharatia had been ousted brutally and cruelly". The High Court Division also noticed that the plaintiff' was forcibly ousted and the Sub- Divisional Officer "appointed the Magistrate, defendant No.3 to go to the spot and give deli very of possession of the Shop No.3 to the defendant Nos. 4 to 7". But curiously enough the High Court Division exonerated the defendants 1 to 3 "as they had no personal interest in the matter except that they wanted to have the cause of defendants 4 to 7 being fulfilled". In this view of the matter the decree was upheld and the suit was dismissed as against the other defendants namely 1, 2, 3, 8 and 9. 

 8. Here is the key to the problem. The transferee is defendant No. 4. He did not claim gum of rent. Nor the plaintiff paid any rout to him Now if the plaintiff had no reason to believe that such transfer has been made as mentioned in the notice Ext. 3 dated 15 9.72 he ought to have made enquiry and pay rent. But in this case plaintiff never paid any rent either to the Pourashava or to the defendant No. 4. He was simply a trespasser. Even after his eviction on 6 5.73 he sat quite over 4 months' time and then brought the suit the suit is for declaration of his tenancy. We have searched in vain as to whose tenancy was declared for giving the restoration of possession. On the face of the deed of relinquishment Ext 4 the plaintiff could not be the tenant of defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 1 said so clearly that he ceased to be its tenant. This notice was the notice contemplated under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act The High Court Division unfortunately observed that though notice under section 106 was not served upon the plaintiff Ext. 3 is clearly that notice, namely, that the plaintiff will have to enter into a new agreement "অন্যথায় ছাড়িয়া দিতে হইবে ". There is the termination notice. Once this notice had been served which is not denied by the plaintiff, the only question is has he attorney the defendant No. 4 as landlord? The answer is in the negative. Then the question whether he has paid any rent for those periods to the defendant No. 1 Pourashava? The answer again is in the negative. He being a tenant whose title was he setting up? If it is title of defendant No. 1 then they have served a notice of relinquishment Ext. 4. In this setting of fact, it is very unfortunate that such a suit was decreed by giving declaration of tenancy and restoration. 

 9. The next question—Where the plaintiff was thrown forcibly. He has disowned his own receipt Ext. 2 by saying that it has been intoned from him forcibly. The persons responsible for such extortion are the defendants 2 and 3 namely, Pourashava, its Administration and the Magistrate but curiously enough the High Court Division exonerated them by saying that they were not doing such work "in, their personal" interest and upheld the view of the trial court for not decreeing the suit against them. If an action is illegal as the High "Court Division found in this case, then illegal action must be rectified. The High Court Division has given an inconsistent finding. The authorities in pursuance of the requisition of the Pourashava under Ordinance XXVI of 1970 (Government and Local Authority Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1970 took the action which confers powers upon the authority for recovering the possession of Government and Local Authority and eviction of unauthorized occupants. Pourashava is a Local Authority (Vide P.O. No. 147 of 1972.) The Pourashava intended to hand over the possession of the premises to the transferee and the plaintiff was requested to enter into a new agreement with the transferee defendant No. 4 or else to vacate the premise but plaintiff did neither. So the law had to take its own course. "Unauthorized occupant" includes (i)................................ (ii) a lessee who continue in possession of the land or building or part thereof after expiry of term or acted under the determination of the lease. Section 3 deals with the eviction of outgoing lessee while section 5 deals with eviction of unauthorized occupant. Section 11 raises a bar to the jurisdiction of Civil Court and section 13 is an indemnifying provision. Such wide powers have been conferred upon the Deputy Commissioner for recovery of possession of the Government and Local authority lands and buildings. The legislature passed such law obviously of necessity. A feeble attempt was made by the respondent’s Counsel that the plaintiff could have been ejected by Civil proceeding. This very contention begs the point for which the Ordinance XXVI of 1970 was passed. In the case of Hasan Ali Vs. Dara Shah, AIR 1936 Nagpur, 282 it was observed: 

 The Pourashava determined the tenancy and relinquished its right title and interest in favour of the defendant. The Pourashava is governed by the T. P. Act. Reliance may be placed on the decision reported in AIR 1928 All 95. Applying these principles in the facts and circumstances of the case there is no hesitation in saying that the plaintiff clearly became a trespasser after the notice dated 15-9•72 and from that time he was simply squatting on the premises without paying any rent to the Pourashava or making any new arrangement with the defendant. The Pourasbava relinquished all its interest in favour of defendant and the plaintiff was informed about it. Still he did not do anything. Then he was asked to vacate the premises. Since he did not do so the Deputy Commissioner sent a Magistrate and police to cause eviction. The plaintiff vacated the premises. After four months he filed the suit for declaration and restoration and compensation. As noticed above, he was a trespasser and he must take the consequence of his illegal action. No relief is available to him in law. The Courts has clearly erred in law in clearing the suit. A trespasser deserves no protection of law. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division having taken the view that the Pourasbava had transferred by these deeds its right, title and interests to defendant No. 4 the plaintiff yet deserved protection by way of a decree which to say the least is an inconsistent stand not supported by law. 

 In the result therefore, this appeal is allowed. Judgment and decree of both the Courts below are set aside and the plaintiffs' suit is dismissed. There will be however no costs.
